stem_md: For  $ \phi: \mathbb{N} \mapsto \mathbb{Z}$  let us define \[ M_{\phi} \equal{} \{f:  \mathbb{N} \mapsto \mathbb{Z}, f(x) > f(\phi(x)), \forall x \in \mathbb{N} \}.\] Prove that if  $ M_{\phi_1} \equal{} M_{\phi_2} \neq \emptyset,$  then  $ \phi_1 \equal{} \phi_2.$  Does this property remain true if \[ M_{\phi} \equal{} \{f:  \mathbb{N} \mapsto \mathbb{N}, f(x) > f(\phi(x)), \forall x \in \mathbb{N} \}?\]
solution_md: Let $\phi \colon \mathbb{N} o \mathbb{N}$ , and for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$ denote by $\phi^n$ the $n$ -th iterate of $\phi$ (with $\phi^0 = extrm{id}_{\mathbb{N}}$ ). For any $x \in \mathbb{N}$ define $\mathcal{O}_{\phi}(x) = \{\phi^n(x) \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ , the orbit of $x$ . In the sequel we will only consider $\phi$ with the property that for any $x \in \mathbb{N}$ the orbit $\mathcal{O}(x)$ is infinite (if even for one $x \in \mathbb{N}$ we would have $\mathcal{O}(x)$ finite, then $M_{\phi} = \emptyset$ , since having $f(x) > f(\phi(x)) > \cdots > f(\phi^n(x)) > \cdots$ leads to a contradiction).**The graph**. Define a directed graph $\overrightarrow{G}_{\phi} = (V_{\phi}, E_{\phi})$ with $V_{\phi} = \mathbb{N}$ and $E_{\phi} = \{(x,y) \equiv \overrightarrow{xy} \mid y = \phi(x)\}$ . The fact that $\mathcal{O}_{\phi}(x)$ is infinite for all $x \in \mathbb{N}$ ensures that $\overrightarrow{G}_{\phi}$ is acyclic. Now, $V_{\phi}$ partitions in the (connected) components of the subjacent undirected graph $G_{\phi}$ . We will denote by $\mathcal{C}_{\phi}(x)$ the component containing $x$ ; clearly $\mathcal{O}_{\phi}(x) \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{\phi}(x)$ , and moreover, for any $y \in \mathcal{C}_{\phi}(x)$ we will have $\mathcal{O}_{\phi}(y) \cap \mathcal{O}_{\phi}(x) eq \emptyset$ . Clearly, $\mathcal{C}_{\phi}(x)$ is a tree (induced) subgraph of $G_{\phi}$ .**The equivalence relation**. The relation $\sim_{\phi}$ defined on $\mathbb{N} imes \mathbb{N}$ by $x \sim_{\phi} y$ if and only if $y \in \mathcal{C}_{\phi}(x)$ is an equivalence relation, with $\hat x = \mathcal{C}_{\phi}(x)$ . **The order relation**. The relation $\prec_{\phi}$ defined on $\mathbb{N} imes \mathbb{N}$ by $x \prec_{\phi} y$ if and only if $x \in \mathcal{O}_{\phi}(y)$ is seen to be a (partial) order relation (it is here that $\mathcal{O}(x)$ is infinite is of paramount importance). We can now define a function $f \colon \mathbb{N} o \mathbb{Z}$ . On each component $\mathcal{C}_{\phi}$ select an arbitrary $x \in \mathcal{C}_{\phi}$ and arbitrarily define $f(x) \in \mathbb{Z}$ . For any $y \in \mathcal{C}_{\phi}$ we will have $\mathcal{O}_{\phi}(y) \cap \mathcal{O}_{\phi}(x) eq \emptyset$ ; take any $z$ from it, thus $z = \phi^{n}(x) = \phi^m(y)$ for some $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$ . Take then $f(y) = f(x) - n + m$ . It is seen that $f$ is coherently defined, and $f(\phi(y)) = f(y) - 1$ , thus $f(y) > f(\phi(y))$ for all $y \in \mathcal{C}_{\phi}$ , and thus for all $y \in \mathbb{N}$ , and so $f \in M_{\phi}$ , therefore $M_{\phi} eq \emptyset$ . Assume now $\phi_1 eq \phi_2$ for some $\phi_1, \phi_2$ as above, i.e. $\phi_1(x) eq \phi_2(x) = y$ for some $x \in \mathbb{N}$ . If $\mathcal{C}_{\phi_1}(y) eq \mathcal{C}_{\phi_1}(x)$ , we can define a function $f \in M_{\phi_1}$ as above, but with $f(x) < f(y) = f(\phi_2(x))$ , thus $f ot \in M_{\phi_2}$ , hence $M_{\phi_1} eq M_{\phi_1}$ . If $\mathcal{C}_{\phi_1}(y) = \mathcal{C}_{\phi_1}(x)$ , then $\mathcal{O}_{\phi_1}(y) \cap \mathcal{O}_{\phi_1}(x) eq \emptyset$ . We can now define a function $f \in M_{\phi_1}$ in a similar manner as above, but with $f(x) < f(y) = f(\phi_2(x))$ , thus $f ot \in M_{\phi_2}$ , hence $M_{\phi_1} eq M_{\phi_1}$ . Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ be minimal such that $z = \phi_1^n (x) \in \mathcal{O}_{\phi_1}(y)$ . If $n=0$ , the above construction will do; if $n\geq 1$ , use different step-values on the branches passing through $x$ and through $y$ , so that $f(x) < f(y)$ . The problem is too much a set-theoretical issue (the reason probably it was not included on the ShortList). What in fact it refers to can be seen as follows The set $M_{\phi}$ is the set of isotone functions $f \colon (\mathbb{N}, \prec_{\phi}) o (\mathbb{Z}, \leq)$ . The problem states that this set of isotone functions determines the partial order relation $\prec_{\phi}$ induced by $\phi$ , since the equality of two such sets, for $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ , leads to the equality of $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ .

stem_md:
An arithmetic function is a real-valued function whose domain is the set of positive integers. Define the convolution product of two arithmetic functions  $ f$  and  $ g$  to be the arithmetic function  $ f * g$ , where \[ (f * g)(n) \equal{} \sum_{ij\equal{}n} f(i) \cdot g(j),\] and  $ f^{*k} \equal{} f * f * \ldots * f$   ( $ k$  times) We say that two arithmetic functions  $ f$  and  $ g$  are dependent if there exists a nontrivial polynomial of two variables  $ P(x, y) \equal{} \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} x^i y^j$  with real coefficients such that

\[ P(f,g) \equal{} \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} f^{*i} * g^{*j} \equal{} 0,\]

and say that they are independent if they are not dependent. Let  $ p$  and  $ q$  be two distinct primes and set

\[ f_1(n) \equal{} \begin{cases} 1 & \text{ if } n \equal{} p, 
0 & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\]

\[ f_2(n) \equal{} \begin{cases} 1 & \text{ if } n \equal{} q, 
0 & \text{ otherwise}. \end{cases}\]

Prove that  $ f_1$  and  $ f_2$  are independent.
solution_md:
I wonder how this problem managed to get into ILL 1989. No more is needed to solve it than directly applying the definition.

It can be easily checked that: $ f_{1}^{*i}*f_{2}^{*j}(n) = \begin{cases}1 \,\,  \text{if} \,\, n=p^{i}q^{j}  0 \,\,  \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $ .

This implies that  $f_1$  and  $f_2$  are independent.

solution_md:
Complete the circle  $\omega$  with diameter  $BC$ . 
Let,  $AC \cap \omega=F$ ,  $D$  be the point on  $\omega$  diametrically opposite to  $F$ , and,  $BT=\frac{1}{3}BC$  where,  $T\in BC$ . Since,  $BC$  is a diameter of  $\omega$  &  $\angle{BCF}=60^\circ$ ,  $F$  is the vertex of a regular hexagon, and, as a result, so is  $D$ .  $\therefore$   $D$  trisects the semi-circular arc  $\Gamma$ . So, it suffices to show that,  $D$  lies on  $AT$ .
Now,
( $\because BF \perp AC$ ),  $BD=CF=\frac{1}{2}AC$   $\Rightarrow \frac{BD}{AC}=\frac{1}{2}=\frac{BT}{TC}$  &  $\angle{DBT}=\angle {TCA}=60^\circ$  (Regular-Hexagon Property).  $\therefore \bigtriangleup{TBD}\sim \bigtriangleup{TBC} \Rightarrow \angle{BTD}=\angle{CTA} \Rightarrow$   $A$ ,  $T$ ,  $D$  are co-linear.

solution_md: I hold in my hands the IMO 1989 LongList brochure, which allows me to correct the statement as being For each sequence $s= (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$ of nonzero natural prime numbers, $ \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ ordered in an arbitrary way, denote by $ f(s)$ the absolute minimum value of the difference of two consecutive numbers of $ s.$ Find the maximum value of $ f(s)$ (for all sequences $s$ with the given properties). - proposed by Vietnam. I doubt the word "prime" has anything to do with this (why then the insistence on the numbers $ \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ , and then the sequences $s$ are widely uncontrollable). I think the problem just wants us to compute $\max_{\sigma \in \mathcal{S}_n} \min_{1\leq k \leq n-1} |\sigma(k+1) - \sigma(k)|$ (where clearly $f(\sigma) = \min_{1\leq k \leq n-1} |\sigma(k+1) - \sigma(k)|$ ). For $n=2m$ even, the example $\sigma = (m+1,1,m+2,2,\ldots,m-1,2m,m)$ has $f(\sigma) = m$ . There cannot exist a $\tau$ with $f(\tau) \geq m+1$ , since $m$ must appear in $\tau$ , and $|m - \ell| \leq m$ for all $1\leq \ell \leq 2m$ . For $n=2m+1$ odd, the example $\sigma = (m+1,1,m+2,2,\ldots,m-1,2m,m,2m+1)$ has $f(\sigma) = m$ . There cannot exist a $\tau$ with $f(\tau) \geq m+1$ , since $m+1$ must appear in $\tau$ , and $|m - \ell| \leq m$ for all $1\leq \ell \leq 2m$ . Therefore the sought after value is $\max_{\sigma \in \mathcal{S}_n} \min_{1\leq k \leq n-1} |\sigma(k+1) - \sigma(k)| = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ .

stem_md: Find the maximum number  $ c$  such that for all  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  to have \[ \{n \cdot \sqrt{2}\} \geq \frac{c}{n}\] where  $ \{n \cdot \sqrt{2}\} \equal{} n \cdot \sqrt{2} \minus{} [n \cdot \sqrt{2}]$  and  $ [x]$  is the integer part of  $ x.$  Determine for this number  $ c,$  all  $ n \in \mathbb{N}$  for which  $ \{n \cdot \sqrt{2}\} \equal{} \frac{c}{n}.$
solution_md:
Let  $ [n\sqrt 2] \equal{} m$ , then  $ 2n^2 \minus{} m^2 \equal{} a\ge 1$  There are infinitely many solutions  $ m^2 \minus{} 2n^2 \equal{} \minus{} 1$ .
Therefore for such  $n$  we get  $ \{n\sqrt 2\} \equal{} \sqrt {m^2 \plus{} 1} \minus{} m \equal{} n\sqrt {2} \minus{} \sqrt {2n^2 \minus{} 1} \equal{} \frac {\sqrt {2}}{4n}(1 \plus{} \frac {1}{4n^2} \plus{} \frac {3}{16n^4} \plus{} \cdots)$ . Therefore the best coefficient is  $ c \equal{} \frac {\sqrt 2}{4}$ , and  $ \{n\sqrt 2\} > \frac {\sqrt 2}{4n} \ \forall n\in N$ .

solution_md: **Solution**: Note that, since $\omega$ is a third root of unity not equal to $1$ , we have that \[ \omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0. \]Substitute $ z \rightarrow \omega z + a $ in the original equation to get the following transformation: \[ f(z) + f(\omega z + a) = g(z) \implies f(\omega z + a) + f(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a) = g(\omega z + a). \]We make the same substitution again: \[ f(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a) + f (\omega^3 z + \omega^2 a + \omega a + a) = g(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a). \]Recall that $ \omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0 $ and $ \omega^3 = 1 $ , so we obtain: \[ f(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a) + f(z) = g(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a). \]Adding the three recent equations together, we get: \[ f(z) + f(\omega z + a) + f(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a) = \dfrac {g(z) + g(\omega z + a) + g(\omega^2 z + \omega a + a}{2}. \]We subtract from the second equation and we get: \[ f(z) = \dfrac {g(z) - g(\omega z + a) + g (\omega^2 z + \omega a + a)}{2}. \]We see that there is a one-to-one bijection between $f$ and $g$ here, in the sense that for every $g$ , there is a unique $f$ . That is, there is exactly one function $f(z)$ , given $g(z)$ , which satisfies the original functional equation. This was exactly what we wanted to show. $ \blacksquare $

stem_md: The incenter of the triangle  $ ABC$  is  $ K.$  The midpoint of  $ AB$  is  $ C_1$  and that of  $ AC$  is  $ B_1.$  The lines  $ C_1K$  and  $ AC$  meet at  $ B_2,$  the lines  $ B_1K$  and  $ AB$  at  $ C_2.$  If the areas of the triangles  $ AB_2C_2$  and  $ ABC$  are equal, what is the measure of angle  $ \angle CAB?$
solution_md:
The incenter of the triangle $ ABC$ is $ K.$ The midpoint of $ AB$ is $ C_1$ and that of $ AC$ is $ B_1.$ The lines $ C_1K$ and $ AC$ meet at $ B_2,$ the lines $ B_1K$ and $ AB$ at $ C_2.$ If the areas of the triangles $ AB_2C_2$ and $ ABC$ are equal, what is the measure of angle $ \angle CAB?$
SolutionLet the tangency points between the incircle with $ AB$ and $ AC$ respectively be $ D$ and $ E$ . Let the midpoints of $ CD$ and $ BE$ be $ Y$ and $ X$ respectively. Furthermore, let the semiperimeter of $ \triangle ABC$ be $ s$ , $ AB \equal{} c$ , $ BC \equal{} a$ , and $ AC \equal{} b$ . It is well-known that $ B_1$ , $ X$ , and $ K$ are collinear as are $ C_1$ , $ Y$ , and $ K$ . Notice that\[ 1\equal{}\frac {[AB_2C_2]}{[ABC]} \equal{} \frac {\frac {AC_2\cdot AB_2\sin \angle BAC}{2}}{\frac {AB\cdot AC\sin \angle BAC}{2}} \equal{} \frac {AC_2}{AB}\cdot \frac {AB_2}{AC}\]Apply Menelaus to $ \triangle AEB$ with transversal $ C_2XB_1$ , we have that $ \frac {AC_2}{C_2B}\cdot \frac {BX}{XE}\cdot \frac {EB_1}{AB_1} \equal{} 1$ . We have that $ BX \equal{} XE$ , so\[ \frac {AC_2}{C_2B} \equal{} \frac {AB_1}{EB_1} \equal{} \frac {\frac {b}{2}}{\frac {b}{2} \minus{} (s \minus{} a)} \equal{} \frac {b}{b \minus{} (a \plus{} b \plus{} c \minus{} 2a)} \equal{} \frac {b}{a \minus{} c}\]which means that $ \frac {C_2B}{AC_2} \equal{} \frac {a \minus{} c}{b}$ , so $ \frac {AB}{AC_2} \equal{} 1 \plus{} \frac {C_2B}{AC_2} \equal{} \frac {a \plus{} b \minus{} c}{b}$ . Similarly, $ \frac {AC}{AB_2} \equal{} \frac {a \plus{} c \minus{} b}{c}$ , so\[ 1 \equal{} \frac {AC}{AB_2}\cdot \frac {AB}{AC_2} \equal{} \frac {a^2 \minus{} (b \minus{} c)^2}{bc} \equal{} \frac {a^2 \minus{} b^2 \minus{} c^2 \plus{} 2bc}{bc}\]\[ bc \equal{} a^2 \minus{} b^2 \minus{} c^2 \plus{} 2bc\]\[ a^2 \equal{} b^2 \plus{} c^2 \minus{} bc\]\[ \cos \angle BAC \equal{} \frac {b^2 \plus{} c^2 \minus{} a^2}{2bc} \equal{} \frac {1}{2} \equal{} \cos 60\]from which it follows that $ \angle BAC \equal{} 60$ .

stem_md: An eccentric mathematician has a ladder with  $ n$  rungs that he always ascends and descends in the following way: When he ascends, each step he takes covers  $ a$  rungs of the ladder, and when he descends, each step he takes covers  $ b$  rungs of the ladder, where  $ a$  and  $ b$  are fixed positive integers. By a sequence of ascending and descending steps he can climb from ground level to the top rung of the ladder and come back down to ground level again. Find, with proof, the minimum value of  $ n,$  expressed in terms of  $ a$  and  $ b.$
solution_md:
Solved with **Aayuu**

We claim that the answer is  $\boxed{a+b-\gcd (a,b)}$ .

By bezout's lemma we may find  $x,y \geq 0$  with  $ax-by=\gcd(a,b)$ . Then we have  $b(y+1)-a(x-1)=a+b-\gcd(a,b)$ , and it is clear that we can perform such a sequence of moves (if we are ever "stuck" then we would have  $ka<b$  which is obviously impossible). This shows that the answer works.

Suppose now that we have  $n<a+b-1$ . Considering all the moves in total, we have  $ax=by$  for some  $x,y \in\mathbb{Z}$ , which implies that we move down atleast  $a$  times and similarly move up atleast  $b$  times. Since  $\gcd(a,b)=1$ ,  $b \cdot k$  (for  $k \in \{0,1,\dots,a-1\})$  forms a complete residue system modulo  $a$ , so we would necessarily have the height be  $b-1 \pmod a$  at some point. But since  $n<a+b-1$ , we have no legal move at this point which is obviously a contradiction.

This completes the proof and we are done.  $\blacksquare$

In the coordinate plane a rectangle with vertices  $ (0, 0),$   $ (m, 0),$   $ (0, n),$   $ (m, n)$  is given where both  $ m$  and  $ n$  are odd integers. The rectangle is partitioned into triangles in such a way that

*(i)* each triangle in the partition has at least one side (to be called a “good” side) that lies on a line of the form  $ x \equal{} j$  or  $ y \equal{} k,$  where  $ j$  and  $ k$  are integers, and the altitude on this side has length 1;

*(ii)* each “bad” side (i.e., a side of any triangle in the partition that is not a “good” one) is a common side of two triangles in the partition.

Prove that there exist at least two triangles in the partition each of which has two good sides.
solution_md: Color the rectangle with the standard black and white rectangle coloring. Call the **offset** of a triangle in the configuration the area of it which is black minus the area of it which is white. Call a triangle **excellent** if it has two good sides, and **plain** otherwise.**Lemma.** The offset of an excellent triangle is  $\pm \frac12$ , and the offset of a plain triangle is  $0$ .**Proof.** This is a simple computation for excellent triangles. As for plain triangles, just split the plain triangle in half with the altitude of length  $1$ , and use the same computations from before. $\blacksquare$ Since the "overall offset" of the entire rectangle is  $1$ , there must clearly be at least  $2$  excellent triangles, so we're done. $\square$

stem_md:
Unit cubes are made into beads by drilling a hole through them along a diagonal. The beads are put on a string in such a way that they can move freely in space under the restriction that the vertices of two neighboring cubes are touching. Let  $ A$  be the beginning vertex and  $ B$  be the end vertex. Let there be  $ p \times q \times r$  cubes on the string  $ (p, q, r \geq 1).$ 

*(a)* Determine for which values of  $ p, q,$  and  $ r$  it is possible to build a block with dimensions  $ p, q,$  and  $ r.$  Give reasons for your answers.
*(b)* The same question as (a) with the extra condition that  $ A \equal{} B.$
solution_md:
Solution from *Twitch Solves ISL*: For (a), the answer is always yes; whereas for (b), the answer is only if at least two of  $p$ ,  $q$ ,  $r$  are even.

Let the box  $\mathcal B$  be located in space spanning  $(0,0,0)$  to  $(p,q,r)$ . Then the string can move from  $(x,y,z)$  to  $(x \pm 1, y \pm 1, z \pm 1)$ . So, the string is going to visit only points of two parity classes in  ${\mathbb F}_2 \times {\mathbb F}_2 \times {\mathbb F}_2$ , say  $(\varepsilon_x \bmod 2, \varepsilon_y \bmod 2, \varepsilon_z \bmod 2)$  and  $(1+\varepsilon_x \bmod 2, 1+\varepsilon_y \bmod 2, 1+\varepsilon_z \bmod 2)$ . However, every unit cube has a string through it, so we find that the string visits every point of this form in  $\mathcal B$ . Let us denote the set of points by  $V$  (which depends on the choice of  $(\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y, \varepsilon_z)$ ).
Hence the question is asking when we can have a Eulerian path or circuit on the resulting graph  $G$  (whose vertex set is  $V$  and whose edges are the string).
However, the degrees of vertices of  $G$  are always even *except* for the corners of  $\mathcal B$ , i.e.\ the eight points \[ 	\Big\{ (0,0,0), \; (p,0,0), \; (0,q,0), \; (0,0,r), \; 	(p,q,0), \; (p,0,r), \; (0,q,r), \; (p,q,r) \Big\}. \]  	
- We can always ensure there are at most 	two corners in  $V$  	by choosing  $\varepsilon_x$ ,  $\varepsilon_y$ ,  $\varepsilon_z$  randomly; 	the expected number of corners is  $\frac14 \cdot 8 = 2$ .
- We can ensure there are zero corners 	if at least two of  $(p,q,r)$  are even; 	otherwise we cannot.

Hence by the classical theorem on Eulerian paths and circuits, (a) is possible always, (b) is possible when at least two of  $(p,q,r)$  are even.

     but it is impossible to form a closed path.
Hence, in part (a), a box can be made of all (p, q, r) and in part (b) only
those (p, q, r) where at least two of the numbers are even.

stem_md: Prove that every integer  $ k$  greater than 1 has a multiple that is less than  $ k^4$  and can be written in the decimal system with at most four different digits.
solution_md:
Let n be the unique integer such that 2n−1 ≤ k < 2n. Let S(n) be the set
of numbers less than 10n that are written with only the digits {0, 1} in
the decimal system. Evidently |S(n)| = 2n > k and hence there exist two
numbers x, y ∈ S(n) such that k | x − y.
Let us show that w = |x − y| is the desired number. By definition k | w.
We also have
w < 1.2 · 10n−1 ≤ 1.2 · (23√2)n−1 ≤ 1.2 · k3√k ≤ k4.
Finally, since x, y ∈ S(n), it follows that w = |x−y| can be written using
only the digits {0, 1, 8, 9}. This completes the proof.

stem_md:
Let  $ n$  be a composite natural number and  $ p$  a proper divisor of  $ n.$  Find the binary representation of the smallest natural number  $ N$  such that 

\[ \frac{(1 \plus{} 2^p \plus{} 2^{n\minus{}p})N \minus{} 1}{2^n}\]

is an integer.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We're looking for the multiplicative inverse of  $ 1+2^{p}+2^{n-p}$  mod  $ 2^n$ .

Case 1:  $ \frac{n}{p}$  is odd.

The inverse is  $ 1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots -2^{n-2p}+2^n$  because

\begin{align*}(1+2^p+2^{n-p})(1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots -2^{n-2p}+2^n)&\equiv (1+2^p+2^{n-p})(1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots -2^{n-2p})
&\equiv (1+2^p)(1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots -2^{n-2p}) + 2^{n-p}
&\equiv 1-2^{n-p}+2^{n-p}
&\equiv 1\mod 2^n\end{align*}

Case 2:  $ \frac{n}{p}$  is even.

The inverse is  $ 1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots+2^{n-2p}-2^{n-p+1}+2^n$  because $ (1+2^p+2^{n-p})(1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots+2^{n-2p}-2^{n-p+1}+2^n)
\equiv (1+2^p+2^{n-p})(1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots+2^{n-2p}-2^{n-p+1})
\equiv (1+2^p)(1-2^p+2^{2p}-2^{3p}+\cdots+2^{n-2p}-2^{n-p+1}) + 2^{n-p}
\equiv 1+2^{n-p} -2^{n-p+1} + 2^{n-p}
\equiv 1+2^{n-p+1}-2^{n-p+1}
\equiv 1\mod 2^n$ Now that we have found these inverses, we can use the fact that, for  $ y>x$ ,  $ 2^{y}-2^{x}=2^{x}+2^{x+1}+\cdots +2^{y-1}$  to write these inverses as the sums of powers of two directly.</details>

stem_md: Ten localities are served by two international airlines such that there exists a direct service (without stops) between any two of these localities and all airline schedules offer round-trip service between the cities they serve. Prove that at least one of the airlines can offer two disjoint round trips each containing an odd number of landings.
solution_md:
Ten localities are served by two international airlines such that there exists a direct service (without stops) between any two of these localities and all airline schedules offer round-trip service between the cities they serve. Prove that at least one of the airlines can offer two disjoint round trips each containing an odd number of landings.
Graph theoretic interpretation : Take a $K_10$ graph (10 vertices and each pair of vertices has an edge between them) color each edge either blue or red (these represent the airlines respectively). We wish to show that there exist 2 disjoint odd monochromatic cycles.***Solution:*** (slightly similar to @Gamamal) We know that since $10>R(3,3)=6$ (where $R$ refers to ramsey numbers), there must exist a monochromatic triangle. WLOG let it be blue colored. Now, delete these three vertices from the graph. We now wish to show that there exists either an odd blue cycle or $2$ disjoint odd red cycles on the remaining $K_7$ graph. If there exists a blue odd cycle, we are done, so assume not. Now we know that $K_7$ is not bipartite so there must exist an odd cycle and since $7>R(3,3)=6$ , There infact exist multiple red triangles . Now delete $3$ vertices of a red cycle such that in the resulting graph all the blue edges are incident to a single vertex, which is clearly possible otherwise if in all the sub-graphs of $4$ vertices there are two blue edges that are not adjacent, it is possible to show that we must have multiple edges that are blue and that there does exist a blue triangle, which is a contradiction to our assumptions.
ProofConsider 4 vertices $A,B,C,D$ and WLOG let the (atleast) 2 blue non-adjacent edges be crossing i.e. $AC,BD$ (like the diagonals of a square). Now consider another pair of vertices $E,F$ and the subgraph $CDEF$ which must have blue $EF$ since $CD$ is blue. But now consider $CBEF$ and $ABEF$ in which $CB$ and $AB$ must also be blue. But this implies that $ABC$ is a blue triangle, contradiction $\blacksquare$
Finally we now have a $K_4$ graph which must have an odd cycle (not necessarily monochromatic) since complete graphs are non-bipartite. But note that the number of blue edges must be $\leq 3$ by Turan's theorem since there doesn't exist any blue triangle here (by assumption). Now there are three cases (number of blue edges $=1,2,3$ ) and in each one it is easy to verify (by constructing edges WLOG) that there infact does exist a red triangle and we are done.

stem_md: Find all natural numbers  $ n$  for which every natural number whose decimal representation has  $ n \minus{} 1$  digits  $ 1$  and one digit  $ 7$  is prime.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Yay big numbers</summary>So, clearly  $n=1,2$  work.

Also, no  $n$  divisible by  $3$  can work, as all such  $n$ -digit numbers are divisible by  $3$ .

For odd  $n$ , consider
   $71...1=6\cdot10^{n-1}+\frac{10^n-1}{9}=\frac{54\cdot10^{n-1}+10^n-1}{9}=\frac{64\cdot10^{n-1}-1}{9}=\left(\frac{8\cdot10^{\frac{n-1}{2}}+1}{9}\right)\left(8\cdot10^{\frac{n-1}{2}}-1\right)$ , which is thus not prime.

So now we've shown that  $1,2$  work, and that  $3,5,6,7,9,11,12...$  don't. The only numbers left to disprove are those of the form  $6k+4$  and  $6k+8$  for natural  $k$ .

In the former case, consider the number  $1....17111=1...1\cdot10^4+7111$ . This can be expressed as $111111\cdot(\text{a big number } b)+7111=13(8547b)+13(547)$  which is divisible by  $13$  and not prime.

As for the latter case, consider  $1...1\cdot10^8 + 11111711=111111(b)+11111711=13(8547b)+13(854747)$  which is again divisible by  $13$ .

Thus, only  $\boxed{n=1,2}$  work.</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Assume one such line exists. First, scale this line so that the the coordinates are integers. Now, we can represent each edge of this broken line as a vector  $ (x,y)$  with  $ x$  and  $ y$  and magnitude  $ d$ . The sum of all these vectors will be  $ (0,0)$ . Call these vectors $ (x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2),...,(x_n,y_n)$ .

where  $ n$  is odd. Then  $ x_1^2 \plus{} y_1^2 \equal{} x_2^2 \plus{} y_2^2 \equal{} ... \equal{} x_n^2 \plus{} y_n^2 \equal{} d^2$ .

Suppose that at least one of  $ x_1,x_2,...,x_n,y_1,y_2,...,y_n$  is odd. Otherwise, we can divide all of the coordinates and  $ d$  by  $ 2$ . Now, because  $ x_1 \plus{} x_2 \plus{} \cdots \plus{} x_n \equal{} 0$  and  $ y_1 \plus{} y_2 \plus{} \cdots \plus{} y_n \equal{} 0$ , an even number of  $ x_1,x_2,...,x_n$  are odd and an even number of  $ y_1,y_2,...,y_n$  are odd.

Now I will show that  $ d$  is even. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that  $ d$  is odd. Then for each pair  $ (x_i,y_i)$ , exactly one of  $ x_i$  and  $ y_i$  is odd. So there are exactly  $ n$  coordinates which are odd, which is a contradiction since we showed above that the number of odd coordinates is even. Hence  $ d$  is even, so  $ d^2\equiv 0\mod 4$ .

But we are also assuming that there is at least one odd coordinate, so for some  $ i$ , we have  $ x_i^2 \plus{} y_i^2\equiv 1$  or  $ 2\mod 4$ , a contradiction.

Note this generalizes to where  $ d^2$  is any integer, not necessarily that  $ d$  is an integer. There is some pair  $ (x_i,y_i)$  with  $ x_i,y_i$  odd, and there is some pair  $ (x_j,y_j)$  (since otherwise every coordinate is odd), so  $ x_i^2 \plus{} y_i^2\not\equiv x_j^2 \plus{} y_j^2\mod 4$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $ p(x)$  be a cubic polynomial with rational coefficients.  $ q_1$ ,  $ q_2$ ,  $ q_3$ , ... is a sequence of rationals such that  $ q_n \equal{} p(q_{n \plus{} 1})$  for all positive  $ n$ . Show that for some  $ k$ , we have  $ q_{n \plus{} k} \equal{} q_n$  for all positive  $ n$ .
solution_md:
Suppose that  $ p(x) = 1/e(ax^{3} + bx^{2} + cx + d) $  where  $ a,b,c,d,e \in \mathbb{Z} $ , $ e > 0 $ . Then suppose that  $ m,M \in \mathbb{Z} $ ,  $ n,N \in \mathbb{N} $ , the fractions $ \frac{m}{n} $  ,  $ \frac{M}{N} $  are reduced and  $ p(\frac{m}{n}) = \frac{M}{N} $ .
But  $ p(\frac{m}{n}) = \frac{am^{3}  +  bm^{2}n + cmn^{2} + dn^{3}}{en^{3}} $ .
Suppose  $ k = gcd(am^{3}  +  bm^{2}n + cmn^{2} + dn^{3},en^{3}) $ . Denote also $ x = am^{3} $ ,  $ y = bm^{2}n + cmn^{2} + dn^{3} $ . Then  $ k | x+y $  and  $ k | en^{3} $ .
Therefore  $ k | e(x^{3} + y^{3}) $  ( because  $ x+y | x^{3} + y^{3} ) $  , but $ k | en^{3} | ey^{3} $ , so  $ k | ex^{3} = ea^{3}m^{9} $  , and as before  $ k | en^{3} $ .
So, at the end,  $ k | ea^{3}m^{9} , ea^{3}n^{3} $ . But  $ gcd(m^{9},n^{3}) = 1 $ , therefore $ k | ea^{3} $ . So we get that  $ gcd(am^{3}  +  bm^{2}n + cmn^{2} + dn^{3},en^{3}) | ea^{3} $ ,
therefore  $ Mea^{3} \geqslant en^{3} $  , so  $ n \leqslant a \sqrt[3]{M} $  .

Now suppose we have a sequence of rational numbers  $ q_{1},q_{2}, \ldots $  such that $ q_{n} = p(q_{n+1}) $ . Write  $ q_{n} = \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} $  as a reduced fraction
where  $ a_{n},b_{n} \in \mathbb{Z} $ ,  $ b_{n} > 0 $ . Then, as we saw before, $ b_{n+1} \leqslant a \sqrt[3]{b_{n}} $ . Therefore the sequence  $ \{ b_{n} \} $  is
bounded. Also note that the sequence  $ \{ q_{n} \} $  is bounded. Indeed, there exists
some  $ C > 0 $  such that for every  $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ ,  $ |x| > C $  we have $ |p(x)| > 2|x| $ . Therefore it is impossible that  $ |q_{n}| > C $  for infinitely many $ n $ 's, because  $ q_{1} $  is bounded.
So  $ \{ b_{n} \} $  is bounded and  $ \{ q_{n} \} $  is bounded, therefore  $ \{ a_{n} \} $ 
is bounded. Therefore the sequence  $ q_{n} $  takes only a finite number of values.
Therefore there exists a rational number  $ q $ , which appears in the sequence  $ \{ q_{n} \} $ 
infinitely many times. Because the number  $ q $  appears at least two times, there is $ k \in \mathbb{N} $ , such that $ \underbrace{p \circ p \circ \ldots \circ p}_{k times} (q) = q $ . Therefore $ k $  is a period for  $ q_{n} $ , because there exists  $ N $  as large as we want,
such that  $ q_{N} = q $ , so because of  $ q_{n-1} = p(q_{n}) $ , we get that $ q_{n-k} = q_{n} $  for every  $ k+1 \leqslant n \leqslant N $ . So because we can take  $ N $ 
to be as large as we want, we get that  $ q_{n-k} = q_{n} $  for every $ k+1 \leqslant n $ .
Therefore  $ q_{n} $  is periodic.

stem_md: Prove that  $ \sum_{k \equal{} 0}^{995} \frac {( \minus{} 1)^k}{1991 \minus{} k} {1991 \minus{} k \choose k} \equal{} \frac {1}{1991}$
solution_md: Multiply both sides by 1991 so  $\sum_{k=0}^{995} (-1)^k \frac{k}{1991-k} {1991-k \choose k} + \sum_{k=0}^{995} (-1)^k {1991-k \choose k}=1$  and reduce the sum to  $\sum_{k=0}^{996} (-1)^k {1992-k \choose k}=1$ . Now define  $S_n = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k{n-k \choose k}$ . We can define this recursively by  $S_n = S_{n-1}-S_{n-2}$ . So we want to find  $S_{1992}$ . Check that  $S_1=1$  and  $S_2=0$  so  $S_3=-1$ ,  $S_4=-1$ ,  $S_5=0$ ,  $S_6=1$ ,  $S_7=1$ , so the sequence is periodic with period 6. But 6 divides 1992 so we're done.

A circle of radius  $\rho$  is tangent to the sides  $AB$  and  $AC$  of the triangle  $ABC$ , and its center  $K$  is at a distance  $p$  from  $BC$ .

*(a)* Prove that  $a(p - \rho) = 2s(r - \rho)$ , where  $r$  is the inradius and  $2s$  the perimeter of  $ABC$ .
*(b)* Prove that if the circle intersect  $BC$  at  $D$  and  $E$ , then
\[DE=\frac{4\sqrt{rr_1(\rho-r)(r_1-\rho)}}{r_1-r}\]

where  $r_1$  is the exradius corresponding to the vertex  $A.$
solution_md:
$2[ABC]=2sr$ , and  $2[ABC]=ap+(b+c)\rho=2s\rho+a(p-\rho)$ , thus  $a(p-\rho)=2s(r-\rho)$ , and we are done with (a). 

From (a), we get  $p=\frac{2s(r-\rho)}{a}+\rho$ . Note that  $KD=KE=\rho$ , thus  $DE=2\sqrt{\rho^2-p^2}$ . Also note that  $[ABC]=sr=(s-a)r_1$ , so  $s=\frac{ar_1}{r_1-r}$ . Substitute it, we get  $p=\frac{2r_1(r-\rho)}{r_1-r}+\rho$ . Now substitute this into  $DE$ , we get  $DE=2\sqrt{\rho^2-\left(\frac{2r_1(r-\rho)}{r_1-r}+\rho\right)^2}=\frac{4\sqrt{rr_1(\rho-r)(r_1-\rho)}}{r_1-r}$ , and we are done.

In a triangle, a symmedian is a line through a vertex that is symmetric to the median with the respect to the internal bisector (all relative to the same vertex). In the triangle  $ABC$ , the median  $m_a$  meets  $BC$  at  $A'$  and the circumcircle again at  $A_1$ . The symmedian  $s_a$  meets  $BC$  at  $M$  and the circumcircle again at  $A_2$ . Given that the line  $A_1A_2$  contains the circumcenter  $O$  of the triangle, prove that:

*(a)* $\frac{AA'}{AM} = \frac{b^2+c^2}{2bc} ;$ *(b)* $1+4b^2c^2 = a^2(b^2+c^2)$
solution_md:
In $\triangle ABC$ , the $A$ -median meets $BC$ at $M$ and the circumcircle again at $A_1$ . The $A$ -symmedian meets $BC$ at $S$ and the circumcircle again at $A_2$ . Prove that $s_a=\frac {2bc}{b^2+c^2}\cdot m_a$ and $O\in A_1A_2\iff (b^2+c^2)^2+4b^2c^2 = a^2(b^2+c^2)$ $\iff$ $\cos A=-\frac {2bc}{b^2+c^2}=-\frac {AS}{AM}$ $\iff$ $\tan\frac A2=\frac {b+c}{|b-c|}$ .
**Proof.** Observe that $\frac {SB}{c^2}=\frac {SC}{b^2}=\frac {a}{b^2+c^2}$ , $A_1A_2\parallel BC$ , i.e. $BA_2=CA_1$ , $BA_1=CA_2$ and $MS=\frac {a|b^2-c^2|}{2(b^2+c^2)}$ . Using similarities $ABA_2\sim AMC$ , $ACA_2\sim AMB$ and $ABA_1\sim ASC$ $\implies$ $\{\begin{array}{c} AA_1\cdot s_a=AA_2\cdot m_a=bc BA_2=CA_1=\frac {ac}{2m_a} BA_1=\frac {ab^2c}{(b^2+c^2)s_a}\ ,\ CA_2=\frac {ab}{2m_a}\end{array}$ . Observe that $BA_1=CA_2\implies$ $\boxed{s_a=\frac {2bc}{b^2+c^2}\cdot m_a}$ . Observe that $\boxed{O\in A_1A_2}$ $\iff$ $AA_1\perp AA_2$ $\iff$ $AS\perp AM$ $\iff$ $SM^2=m_a^2+s_a^2$ $\iff$ $\frac {a^2(b^2-c^2)^2}{4(b^2+c^2)^2}=m_a^2\cdot\frac {(b^2+c^2)^2+4b^2c^2}{(b^2+c^2)^2}$ $\iff$ $[2(b^2+c^2)-a^2][(b^2+c^2)+4b^2c^2]=a^2(b^2+c^2)^2-4a^2b^2c^2$ $\iff$ $\boxed{(b^2+c^2)^2+4b^2c^2=a^2(b^2+c^2)}$ $\iff$ $(b^2+c^2)(b^2+c^2-a^2)+4b^2c^2=0$ $\iff$ $(b^2+c^2)\cos A+2bc=0$ $\iff$ $\cos A=-\frac {2bc}{b^2+c^2}$ $\iff$ $\boxed{\cos A=-\frac {s_a}{m_a}}$ .
**Generalization.** Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Consider two points $\{M,S\}\subset [BC]$ of $\triangle ABC$ so that $\widehat {BAM}\equiv\widehat {CAS}$ . The lines $AM$ , $AS$ meet again the circumcircle of $ABC$ in $A_1$ , $A_2$ respectively. Prove that $AS=\frac {(m+1)bc}{mb^2+c^2}\cdot AM$ and $\boxed{O\in A_1A_2\iff (mb^2+c^2)^2+(m+1)^2b^2c^2 = a^2(mb^2+c^2)\iff\cos A=-\frac {2mbc}{m^2b^2+c^2}\iff\tan\frac A2=\frac {mb+c}{|mb-c|}}$ .

stem_md: Suppose that points  $X, Y,Z$  are located on sides  $BC, CA$ , and  $AB$ , respectively, of triangle  $ABC$  in such a way that triangle  $XY Z$  is similar to triangle  $ABC$ . Prove that the orthocenter of triangle  $XY Z$  is the circumcenter of triangle  $ABC.$
solution_md:
Beautiful problem! I use spiral similarity.

Let  $A_1, B_1, C_1$  be midpoints of  $BC, CA, AB$  respectively. Then  $\triangle  XYZ \sim \triangle A_1B_1C_1$ . Note that  $O$  (circumcentre of  $ABC$ ) is orthocenter of  $A_1B_1C_1$ . We prove that the center of spiral similarity mapping  $XYZ$  to  $A_1B_1C_1$  is  $O$ . This will be enough as spiral similarity maps orthocenter onto orthocenter.

This spiral similarity  $\phi$  maps  $X \to A_1, Y \to B_1$  and  $Z \to C_1$ . Now take spiral similarity  $\phi'$  which takes  $X \to Y$  and  $A_1 \to B_1$ , but  $\phi'$  is dual to  $\phi$  so they have the same center!

Now just recall the construction of the center of spiral similarity. The center of  $\phi'$  is the intersection of circles  $CA_1B_1$  and  $CXY$ . So our desired center lies on circumcircle of  $\triangle CA_1B_1$  and by analogue also of  $\triangle BA_1C_1$  and  $\triangle AB_1C_1$ . We can easily see, that  $O$  is the unique point with this property ( $AO$  is diameter of the circle  $AB_1OC_1$ ). So we are done!

stem_md:
Given the condition that there exist exactly  $1990$  triangles  $ABC$  with integral side-lengths satisfying the following conditions:
(i)  $\angle ABC =\frac 12 \angle BAC;$ (ii)  $AC = b.$ Find the minimal value of  $b.$ **Attachments:**

![1990.gif](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/f/c/b72f0059467bb6a42703cb282f2a7a4c3b6589)
solution_md:
Claim: [ $0<x<\pi/2$  and the triangle  $\bigtriangleup ABC$  with side lengths  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$ , has angles  $A=2x$ ,  $B=x$ , and  $C=180-3x$ ]  $\iff$  [ $a^2=b(b+c)$  and  $0<c<3b$  and  $0<a<2b$ ]

<details><summary>Proof</summary>We define four propositions below, and our aim is to prove the equivalence of the first and the last.

Proposition  $P_1$ :  $0<x<\pi/2$  and the triangle  $\bigtriangleup ABC$  with side lengths  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$ , has angles  $A=2x$ ,  $B=x$ , and  $C=180-3x$  

Proposition  $P_2$ :  $0<x<\pi/2$  and  $a,b,c>0$  and   $$ \frac{\sin 2x}{a} = \frac{\sin x}{b} = \frac{\sin (180-3x)}{c} $$  Proposition  $P_3$ :  $0<x<\pi/2$  and  $a,b,c>0$  and   $$ \cos x = \frac{a}{2b} $$      $$ \sin^2x = \frac{3b-c}{4b} $$  Proposition  $P_4$ :  $a^2=b(b+c)$  and  $0<c<3b$  and  $0<a<2b$ The equivalence of the first two is simply the law of sines. The equivalence of  $P_2$  and  $P_3$  can be established with the following ingredients:  $\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x$ ,   $\sin (180-3x)= \sin 3x = 3\sin x-4\sin^3x$ , and  $\sin x \neq 0$ . Meanwhile,  $P_3 \Rightarrow P_4$  can be established using  $\cos^2x + \sin^2x = 1$  along with bounds on the trigonometric functions.  $P_4 \Rightarrow P_3$  is given in detail here: We define  $x_1$  and  $x_2$  as the values, which are strictly between  $0$  and  $\frac{\pi}{2}$ , that satisfy the equations below:   $$ \cos x_1 = \frac{a}{2b} $$     $$ \sin^2x_2 = \frac{3b-c}{4b} $$   The fact that  $0<a<2b$  and  $0<c<3b$  ensures existence and uniqueness of both  $x_1$  and  $x_2$ . Using the fact that  $a^2=b(b+c)$ , we can verify that  $\cos^2x_1 + \sin^2x_2 = 1$ , which implies  $x_1=x_2$ , since they are both strictly between  $0$  and  $\frac{\pi}{2}$ .  $P_3$  follows.</details>

The problem then boils down to the following: Given some positive integer  $b$ , how many positive integer solutions does the following system have:  $a^2=b(b+c)$  and  $0<c<3b$  and  $0<a<2b$ .

Claim: If  $s^2$  is the largest square that divides  $b$ , then there are exactly  $s-1$  solutions to the diophantine system, (and therefore,  $s-1$  triangles that satisfy the conditions). Note that this statement implies its converse.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>In searching for solutions, we are really searching for some integer  $(b+c)$  which is bigger than  $b$  (obviously) and which, when multiplied by  $b$ , gives some perfect square, which is less than  $4b^2$ . (The fact that  $0<c<3b$  is necessarily a consequence, so we can ignore it).

Substitute, then,  $(b+c)$  with  $y$ . The solutions for  $y$  are exactly those which satisfy  $b^2<by=a^2<4b^2$ . Suppose the largest square which divides  $b$  is  $s^2$ . Then  $b=s^2p_1p_2...p_n$  where  $p_i$  are distinct primes. Since  $by$  is also a perfect square, we must be able to decompose  $y$  as  $y=r^2p_1p_2...p_n$ . The inequality then gives us:   $$ b^2<by=a^2<4b^2 $$     $$ b<y<4b $$     $$ s^2p_1p_2...p_n < r^2p_1p_2...p_n < 4s^2p_1p_2...p_n $$     $$ s^2<r^2<4s^2 $$     $$ s<r<2s $$   which gives  $s-1$  solutions for  $r$  which correspond to precisely  $s-1$  distinct choices of  $y$  and the corresponding choices for  $c$ . Hence, if  $s^2$  is the largest square that divides  $b$ , then there are exactly  $s-1$  solutions to the diophantine system, and therefore,  $s-1$  triangles that satisfy the conditions.</details>

Hence, if a value of  $b$  yields  $1990$  triangles, the largest square which divides  $b$  is  $1991^2$ . The minimum such  $b$  is  $1991^2$ .

stem_md:
Let function  $f : \mathbb Z_{\geq 0}^0 \to \mathbb N$  satisfy the following conditions:

(i)  $ f(0, 0, 0) = 1;$ (ii)   $f(x, y, z) = f(x - 1, y, z) + f(x, y - 1, z) + f(x, y, z - 1);$ (iii) when applying above relation iteratively, if any of  $x', y', z$ ' is negative, then  $f(x', y', z') = 0.$ Prove that if  $x, y, z$  are the side lengths of a triangle, then   $\frac{\left(f(x,y,z) \right) ^k}{ f(mx ,my, mz)}$  is not an integer for any integers  $k, m > 1.$
solution_md:
We can easily find out  $ f(x, y, z) = \frac{(x+y+z)!}{x!y!z!}$  by some combinatorical method (i.e.  $f(x, y, z)$  is the number of ways that can from  $(0,0,0)$  to  $(x,y,z)$ )
If  $x,y,z$  are side length of the triangle.We have  $2max(mx,my,mz,x+y+z)\le mx+my+mz$ . By Bertrand's Conjecture, a prime must exist between  $max(mx,my,mz,x+y+z)$  and  $mx+my+mz$ , as a result, the prime is divisible by denominator but not divisible by numerator. Therefore  $ \frac{\left(f(x,y,z)\right)^{k}}{ f(mx ,my, mz)} $  is not an integer.

stem_md: $A$  and  $B$  are two points in the plane  $\alpha$ , and line  $r$  passes through points  $A, B$ . There are  $n$  distinct points  $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$  in one of the half-plane divided by line  $r$ . Prove that there are at least  $\sqrt n$  distinct values among the distances  $AP_1, AP_2, \ldots, AP_n, BP_1, BP_2, \ldots, BP_n.$
solution_md: Suppose the distances  $AP_1,...AP_n$  is the set of distinct lengths  $x_1<x_2<...<x_a$  where  $a$  is the no. of different lengths. Similarly  $BP_1,...,BP_n$  are the set of distances  $y_1<...<y_b$  where  $b$  is the no. of distinct lengths. Then all the  $n$  points must lie on one of the intersection of the circles centered  $A,B$  and radius  $x_i,y_j$ . But since there are at most  $ab$  such intersections, we have  $ab\geq n$ . By AM-GM, we have  $\frac{a+b}{2}\geq\sqrt{ab}\geq \sqrt{n}$ . Since the mean of  $a,b$  is at least  $\sqrt{n}$ , one of them, WLOG  $a$ , is at least  $\sqrt{n}$ . Thus we have at least  $a\geq \sqrt{n}$  distances.

stem_md:
Let  $p, k$  and  $x$  be positive integers such that  $p \geq k$  and  $x < \left[ \frac{p(p-k+1)}{2(k-1)} \right]$ , where  $[q]$  is the largest integer no larger than  $q$ . Prove that when  $x$  balls are put into  $p$  boxes arbitrarily, there exist  $k$  boxes with the same number of balls.

**Attachments:**

![1990.gif](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/5/2/83b51ecd11a2a1274eaf67bb8be45f7293744e)
solution_md:
Let's look at it the other way. Suppose we want there to exist *no* set of  $k$  boxes with the same number of balls. What is the least number of balls we could use? Well, we would want to have  $k-1$  boxes to have  $0$  balls,  $k-1$  of them to have 1 ball and so on. Suppose that  $p$  divided by  $k-1$  has a quotient  $q$ . Using this method, the least number of balls,  $x_{\text {min}}$  that we could use is   $$ x_{\text {min}} = \frac{(k-1)(q)(q-1)}{2} + q(p-(k-1)q) = \frac{q}{2}(2p-(q+1)(k-1)) $$   

Now it is just an exercise to show that this exceeds the quantity given in the problem statement. This will imply that if some  $x$  is less than the quantity given, it is also less than this minimum allowed, and therefore there must then be  $k$  boxes with the same number of balls. Let's begin with the following self-evident statement, and work our way down:  $$ (q+1)(k-1)>p $$  <details><summary>Intermediate Steps</summary>$$ q(k-1) > p-k+1 $$    $$ q(k-1)(p-q(k-1)) > (p-k+1)(p-q(k-1)) $$    $$ q(k-1)(p-q(k-1)) + q(k-1)(p-k+1)> (p-k+1)p $$    $$ q(k-1)(2p-(q+1)(k-1)) > (p-k+1)p $$</details>  $$ \frac{q}{2}(2p-(q+1)(k-1)) > \frac{(p-k+1)p}{2(k-1)} \geq \displaystyle \left[ \frac{(p-k+1)p}{2(k-1)}\right] $$   as required.
